name: Vitamin B12
short: Trial (65+, high homocysteine): more cancers on B12 plus folic acid. Cohort: single B12 supplements linked to lung cancer in men. Case series/reports: anaphylaxis (mostly injected), acne-like rashes.
text: In a 2-year randomised placebo-controlled trial in 2919 people aged 65 or over with raised homocysteine, daily vitamin B12 combined with folic acid (both groups also received vitamin D) did not change the total number of adverse events, including deaths, but 63 people in the supplement group and 42 in the placebo group reported a new cancer (hazard ratio 1.56); the authors note the study was not designed to assess cancer, and the result is for the combination, not B12 alone. In an observational cohort of 77,118 adults aged 50-76, use of vitamin B6 and B12 from individual supplements, but not from multivitamins, was associated with a 30% to 40% higher lung cancer risk in men, and men in the highest category of 10-year average B12 supplement dose (above 55 micrograms a day) had almost double the risk of non-users (hazard ratio 1.98), with higher risk in men who smoked; no association was seen in women, and an association does not show cause. Allergic reactions are rare but can be serious: among 29 patients referred to three UK allergy centres for suspected vitamin B12 hypersensitivity, 18 had immediate reactions and 8 had anaphylaxis (7 to injected and 1 to oral vitamin B12), and the authors concluded that confirmed hypersensitivity is rare; a separate case report describes severe anaphylaxis after an intramuscular cyanocobalamin injection in a woman who later took oral vitamin B12 with no adverse effects. Case reports also describe acne-like eruptions, including in a man 6 weeks after starting weekly intramuscular hydroxocobalamin, and in a young woman with pernicious anaemia who, after repeated daily 1 mg oral doses of cyanocobalamin (12 mg in total), developed acne, palpitations, anxiety, restlessness (akathisia), facial flushing, headache and insomnia; she improved two weeks after stopping, and the authors report no sequelae or complications. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
